The tribute will honor Navarrette for her portrayal of Nikki Freeman in Obsession , with her performance and transformation throughout the film showcasing the actress’ range and talent. The Gotham Film & Media Institute created the Spotlight Tribute to celebrate artists whose work in the year’s most successful films had a striking impact on audiences worldwide. articles.title: 'Dig' Review: Amy Poehler and Mike Schur Reunite for Peacock's Likable but Underwhelming Archeology Comedy
articles.summary: Hugh Laurie co-stars as the head of a Greek antiquities dig in this 10-episode series from the 'Parks and Recreation' duo.
articles.content:
According to PsychologistWorld.com, the website most successful at gaming the Google algorithm and therefore appearing first when you search for nocturnal interpretations, dreaming about falling into a pit denotes "deep sorrow."

Perhaps it's the lingering impact of rooting for Boston sports teams in the early '90s, but Michael Schur has a fixation on pits and the consequences of falling into them that probably requires further examination. Dig The Bottom Line Can you dig it? Sure, though maybe not a lot. Airdate: Monday, November 23 Cast: Amy Poehler, Hugh Laurie, Fina Strazza, Geraldine Viswanathan, Antonia Thomas Creators: Mike Schur and Amy Poehler

More than 17 years after a poorly monitored pit supplied the inciting events for NBC's beloved Parks and Recreation , Schur gazes once more into the abyss to trigger the story behind Peacock's Dig , a comedy that might as well be called Parks and Excavation given that its ensemble is led by Parks star Amy Poehler , also a co-creator here. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories TV A Decade After 'Parks and Rec,' Amy Poehler Is Back on TV With 'Dig': "I Was Waiting for the Right Thing" Movies 'Steps' Review: A Stellar Voice Cast Including Amanda Seyfried, Ali Wong and Bette Midler Gets Stuck in a Tortured Revisionist Fairy Tale

It's a comparison that's inevitable and will inevitably spark disappointment; Dig is a pleasantly likable comedy, but it's never hugely funny like Schur's The Good Place (and what is Hell if not a theological pit?) nor is it deeply poignant like Schur's A Man on the Inside (and what is aging if not the existential pit that comes for us all?). It's a minor disappointment. The cast is too good and the vibe too amiable to incite any real antipathy. Still, there's an ideal next gear, be it zaniness or sentiment, that Dig never finds.

Poehler plays Elise, second in command at an archeological dig site in coastal Greece. The various trenches are apparently primarily used as a summer program attracting American undergrads hoping to drink, flirt and occasionally uncover relics from a bygone civilization. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The program is supervised by renowned archeologist Neville Wycombe ( Hugh Laurie ), but he mostly makes morning announcements, absorbs the adulation of the "Ugs" and threatens to retire, only to stick around. It's Elise who makes everything function, but her short fuse and occasional notes of contempt for her young charges render her less than ideal for the top spot she craves.

Elise is slightly more comfortable around the staff, including the privileged Clare ( Antonia Thomas ), who helps curate the trinkets found by the undergraduates. Perhaps Elise's impatience with the younger characters stems from a nebulously bad first marriage — she's now in a perpetual flirtation with the neighboring town's gregarious mayor (Kayvan Novak's Stavros) — or the betrayal of former student Dylan ( Geraldine Viswanathan ), who abruptly left shortly before they were supposed to go start their own dig together five years earlier.

Now Dylan is back, determined to set things right with Elise and with Barry (Jon Pointing), a former flame now engaged to Clare.

Adding confusion and lots of pratfalls is Patty ( Fina Strazza ), a farm girl with limited social skills and an abiding love for Disney movies and mythology. Patty arrives as Neville's new assistant, one of several jobs she really isn't qualified for.

The series, based on Kate Myers' novel Excavations , probably works best as a group hang comedy about people committed to a serious pursuit that isn't always valued by the world at large — you know, a bit like Parks and Recreation . But rather than sticking to the simplicity of a setting that's basically a glorified summer camp, the series complicates things when Elise and Dylan make a discovery that leads to a mystery that turns everything upside down and forces everybody to learn very important lessons about themselves. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Some shots of pretty beaches and white plastered villages aside, most of Dig has a soundstage feeling. Even the archeological trenches themselves are artificial-looking, less than ideal given how much time we spend in them. But Dig quickly becomes more about a mystery with "Don't steal cultural treasures!" as the underpinning than about archeology in literal or even metaphorical form. Schur did far better at mystery-crafting on A Man on the Inside , especially in its first season.

The pilot, which isn't bad (none of the 10 episodes are) but is definitely clunky, introduces us to the main characters pretty much by having other people tell them things about their personalities that they presumably already know.

"I know your default setting is tough love, but please just learn to give people some grace," Neville tells Elise.

"It's like you're from a fairy tale of neglected children lost in the forest," Clare tells Dylan, whose chaotic energy is noticeable even to random baristas.

The problem is that the characters, despite their exposition-heavy introductions, are oddly fuzzy, and the performances don't always match the way the characters are described.

There's a logic to the way Elise, Clare, Dylan and Patty are constructed. They are four women on the cusp of transition. Elise, age unspecified, is wondering if she's ever going to get the opportunity to go from supporting player to the lead in her own life. Clare is 39, and she's wondering if she's ready to step out of the shadow of her mother's wealth and become a grown-up on her own terms. Dylan is 29, and she thinks it's time to develop some maturity. And Patty is 19, kept in perpetual childhood by her upbringing but ready for a lot of life milestones that more mainstream kids experienced five or 10 years earlier. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

It's very tidy, but nothing plays out that clearly. Elise is mean in the pilot, but she's softened so immediately that she just becomes a variation on Poehler's beloved Leslie (almost an anagram of "Elise") Knope, an enthusiast in a job she takes more seriously than her colleagues do. Viswanathan plays Dylan as more loosely flighty than chaotic, which gives her very little room for the taming or development that it's suggested she needs. I never quite got what Clare's personality was supposed to be, because "rich" isn't a real personality. And since Thomas doesn't project as appreciably older than Viswanathan or Strazza, the stratification of these four women, each representing a different decade on life's journey, doesn't really emerge. (I also don't understand what any of the characters do the rest of the year. But I guess I don't understand what Bill Murray's Trapper does when he isn't counseling the kids in Meatballs either. And yes, Dig is basically Meatballs with fossils.)

It's only Strazza ( Paper Girls ) who has a character with a fully discernible arc, written with enough specificity to lead to a fully developed performance. Yes, Patty is a broad and familiar type, but Strazza plays the bumbling naiveté to the hilt and, when the opportunity presents itself, Patty's desire for her first real friend group and her first chance at love let Strazza ground the entire series. It's Strazza's show, so if she annoys you — some viewers will find her too broad, though I did not — that's a problem. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Strazza is responsible for most of my laughs and most of the show's effective emotional beats. I smiled a lot at Viswanathan's inconsistently written, solidly delivered one-liners. Poehler is an entirely appealing straight-woman, and although I didn't find Elise funny, I liked the romantic charge she brought to her scenes with Novak. I appreciated how Novak takes a character who starts off cartoonish and makes him into an odd kind of leading man, one who the series only rarely positions as a leading man. I guess that title goes to Laurie, at his funniest when he treats Neville as a bloviating companion to the actor's adored run as Bertie Wooster on British TV's Jeeves and Wooster .

Greek viewers who took umbrage at the lack of Greeks in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey will have more to be irritated by here: The biggest Greek role goes to the not-even-vaguely-Greek Novak, and there's a heavy reliance on Greek stereotypes (several embodied by the far more Greek and far more amusing Jason Mantzoukas), even if they're introduced to be mocked or debunked. Even Greece itself is played primarily by Italy and Universal Studios in Hollywood. The use of real locations in Greece and Italy comes across more as a pretext for a pleasant getaway for the cast and crew than anything that truly adds authenticity.

Some people will suggest that these are mere quibbles — the inconsistently written characters, sporadic laughs and superficial mystery — and that I had to dig for them. And, surely, the most glaring problem with Dig is its inferiority to previous Schur creations. That's what you get for setting the bar high rather than low, or even somewhere subterranean. A pit, perhaps?

articles.title: 'The Traitors: New Blood' Renewed for Second Season at NBC
articles.summary: The renewal comes just before the show wraps its initial run.
articles.content:
NBC will head back to Scotland for a second season of The Traitors : New Blood .

The network has renewed the show, a civilian spin on Peacock's hit competition show The Traitors . The pickup comes just before New Blood' s first season finale, which will play out over two hours Thursday night.

Alan Cumming , who hosts both U.S. versions of The Traitors , will continue his role in season two of New Bloods and the forthcoming fifth season of the celebrity iteration of the series, which premieres in January on Peacock. Before streaming, The Traitors: New Blood is averaging about 2.9 million viewers over seven days. Cross-platform figures for the full season weren't immediately available, but streaming likely bumps the total up by a significant amount — the series premiere grew to more than 6 million viewers (including on-air repeats) over three days. NBC says the series has "reached" 23 million viewers across all platforms — i.e., that many people have watched at least a minute or two of the show. The network also notes that about 61 percent of those viewers are new to The Traitors franchise.

The Traitors: New Blood is produced by Studio Lambert. Cumming executive produces with Mike Cotton, Sam Rees-Jones, Rosie Franks, Jack Burgess, Stephen Lambert and Tim Harcourt. The Traitors is a Banijay Entertainment format and was created and developed by IDTV in cooperation with RTL Creative Unit.

When the Chroma Awards opened for entries for the first time in 2025, its organizers bet that a global community of AI-native creators was ready for a stage of its own. Now, that stage is getting bigger. ElevenLabs , in partnership with CapCut , Cantina and Runware , has launched the second season of the Chroma Awards, with submissions open to creators worldwide through Jan. 7, 2027. articles.content:
I'm waiting for Andrew Scott in an LA restaurant on an unusually rainy afternoon, thinking about the last time we met, in 2024.

Back then, as we’d chatted in the Deadline podcast studio, I’d asked him, “When was the last time you cried?” And he’d answered, simply, “Today.”

It turned out his mother had died only a few days before. Terrified I’d made an awful time worse for him and wanting to offer support, I’d explained that my dad had passed a few months ago. Another actor might have quickly moved back to the safer topic of work — in this case, his role in the series Ripley — but instead, he’d asked, “How is it, further along?” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

“You get more used to it,” I’d offered, lamely. There’s a quality to Scott that isn’t reserved for meeting him in person, he brings it to his work. And that is the sense that his feelings, the bald truth of his experiences, are right there on the surface, as though they involve us. So, when his latest film, Elsinore , premiered at Toronto, and Scott went deep into a story that skewers the preciousness of life, the inevitability of death and all of our collective losses, I, along with what seemed like the entire theater, simply dissolved .

In the film, Scott plays real-life actor Ian Charleson — a man for whom the phrase ‘rage against the dying of the light’ might have been written. In 1989, when Charleson discovers he’s facing his own imminent death from AIDS-related illness, he’s offered his dream role, and deciding he’d “rather die of Hamlet than AIDS,” he takes to the stage in the ultimate act of defiance.

Scott has been acting since he was eight years old. Ever since his mother, Nora, who was an art teacher, encouraged him to act as a way to get past shyness and a childhood lisp. A successful stage career followed, along with Spielberg's TV miniseries Band of Brothers , a BAFTA-winning Sherlock role as Moriarty and a villain in the Bond film Spectre , among other things. But, it was, of course, Scott's 'hot priest' in Phoebe Waller-Bridge's Fleabag that shot him to major stardom — it seemed everyone, including the critics, craved the forbidden fruit of his clergyman character. After that came Andrew Haigh's All of Us Strangers opposite Paul Mescal and double Emmy nominations for the miniseries Ripley . blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

But it's the past two years, since I last saw him, that his head has to have truly been spinning. He's taken on back-to-back jobs, like the film Blue Moon , Lena Dunham's show Too Much, The Comeback with Lisa Kudrow, the films Wake Up Dead Man and Pressure, and the U.K. TV series It Gets Worse, in which he plays a bonkers therapist. Add to that the marathon of Vanya on stage in both London and Off-Broadway as a one-man show — that's all five parts at once. Then, after Elsinore , he shot upcoming John Crowley-directed film Walk the Blue Fields with Emily Blunt and Ciarán Hinds. Plus Chloe Domont's A Place in Hell with Michelle Williams and Daisy Edgar-Jones and Justine Triet's psychological thriller Fonda. It's a wonder he's had any time to think…

In Elsinore , under Simon Stone ’s direction and with Stephen Beresford ’s screenplay, Scott, who also serves as a producer, is joined by Olivia Colman as Ian’s physician Dr. Margaret Johnson, Billie Piper and Matthew Beard as Ian’s friends Patsy Pollock and Sean Mathias, Johnny Flynn as Hamlet director Richard Eyre , and such greats as Juliet Stevenson, who actually worked with Charleson in multiple stage productions, including The Taming of the Shrew in 1979.

As Scott walks us through heart-piercing parallels between Ian and Hamlet, something like alchemy emerges — a sense that this is a film about all of us, in this moment. What really matters? What would we do, given just weeks to live?

Back at the restaurant, Scott is suddenly standing there, wearing a cheerful sweatshirt with ‘P-Town’ across the front. He opens his arms to hug me, and I know then that he remembers the last time.

What follows is a conversation about grief, the privilege and weight of getting older, how he plans to make the most of it, and why his favorite people live with courage and the daring “to say the unsayable.”

DEADLINE: You are the same age as me. You recently turned 50, right? How do you feel about it?

ANDREW SCOTT: I wasn't looking forward to it. I don't like my birthday anyway.

DEADLINE: Why not? Just the fuss of it, you mean?

SCOTT: I always like a sort of non-event, like the day after a wedding, or getting accidentally drunk on a Tuesday, rather than, "You've got this big thing." They're not necessarily as actually fun as you think they're going to be. And then you've got big things like events with work and everything, that when it comes to my birthday, it feels like another thing to have to do, in some ways. I was working actually on my birthday. I was doing a play. I did this play Sea Wall in New York and I went out for dinner with friends and that was nice. What did you do? Did you do much?

DEADLINE: I didn't want to do anything, but then my friends were like, "Don't be stupid. We are going to make you do something." And it turned out to be the most amazing thing.

SCOTT: Oh, really? Tell me more.

DEADLINE: We rented a house together for a weekend. And it was incredible.

SCOTT: Yeah, that's what I'm going to do when things calm down. I've got to take my friends away. And that's what I like. I did it for my 40th and my 45th. So, I'll do it again. It's gorgeous. I love, as my sister calls it, ‘the long hang.’

DEADLINE: It's a bit like getting married, these birthdays. You have this leverage to make people go somewhere and do something.

SCOTT: Yeah, exactly. I just love the idea you get all the new stuff out of the way and then you're just into having a laugh with people. Just talking and going home and having a drink. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

DEADLINE: When I first saw Elsinore , I did that kind of crying where you feel like your chest hurts. I could not get it together. Red, puffy, blubbering. I thought, OK the second time I watch this film, I'll be fine.

SCOTT: Because you know what’s coming.

DEADLINE: Nope. Absolute carnage, just a total mess. I also experienced it with our last meeting in mind.

SCOTT: Yes, I remember so well.

DEADLINE: Meeting you was the first time that someone had asked me what grief is like a little bit further down the road, because it was so new to me. And I would now say to you that it gets worse.

SCOTT: [Laughs] Yeah, it gets worse.

DEADLINE: The film had such a profound effect on me. Watching Ian really go for his life’s dream against the clock at only 40 is devastating and glorious at the same time. And being 50 now, it’s also because it's the turning point where you start thinking, oh, sh*t.

SCOTT: Yeah, absolutely. You think you just have an awareness of the value of time. And I think it's actually what the film is about. It's about our most valuable asset, which is our time. And what Ian chose to do with it, he chose that he was going to choose quality over quantity, and that actually, this lifelong goal that he had just came right when his taxi was waiting, so to speak. And he got to do this thing right at the very end of the finish line. And that, I think, really affects people. My friend has this great expression, which is ‘little did we know.’ She was like, "Little do we know. We don't know what way it's going to go." Little do we know what's going to happen to us this evening.

At the end of every day, you're able to go, "God, I have no idea that that's what's going to happen." And something new does happen every single day if you choose to keep your antennae on. And I think Ian was very aware that he wanted something new, because I think one of the most insidious things about being ill, as we know, is being in a hospital, waiting outside in waiting rooms, and waiting for results, and lethargy in some ways. So, he used to go to the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, then down to rehearsal, where you are exploring the greatest play that has ever been written about life and death, playing that extraordinary part with these brilliant artists. I mean, in some ways, of course you want to do that. And so, even though people thought that it was going to be the destruction of him, in some ways I think he thought it was going to heal him. And it did, in some ways.

There is another thing they call Dr. Theater, which is a thing where you might have a terrible cold and you're in such a bad mood. You come in and you're like, "Oh my god, I'm not going to be able to do it." And then you go on and you do the play. It's something about the collective imagination of the audience. They don't care about your cold. They don't care about anything else. Plus your imagination and plus the story from start to finish being said in the dark, that your cold and your bad feeling, you just go to a place and you don't feel ill for that time that you're on stage and then you come off and you…

DEADLINE: … puke in a bucket like Ian did.

SCOTT: Exactly. And it's true. I think any actor, particularly in the theater, will tell you about Dr. Theater.

DEADLINE: I've been listening to the audio version of Judi Dench's memoir Is It Too Late to Make a Run For It? In it she talks having to pretend to drink on the stage. Obviously, it's just colored water, but she felt so drunk by the end of it. Have you ever felt like that? The crowd making you feel it?

SCOTT: Yeah. It's definitely a thing, isn't it? It makes you think about the energy of the people that you have in your life and how you break free of things that are just not giving you anything, like this [points to iphone on the table]. That's one thing I think an awful lot about. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

DEADLINE: Yes, my hand is always reaching for the dopamine hit of the phone.

SCOTT: All the time. Sometimes before you're even awake, you have somebody telling you about peptides or micronutrients. Do you know what I mean? Just stuff that you're like, "Whoa." That's what anxiety is — receiving so much information about which you can do very little. That's actually literally kind of textbook anxiety. It's just a time stealer. That's the biggest thing. It's a time stealer and it's not rest. It seems like rest, but it's not.

DEADLINE: What's it like for you to watch this film? Are you able to watch it in an objective way, or is that impossible for you? Is it difficult emotionally?

SCOTT: I do feel emotional about it. I won't watch it anymore. I've seen it enough now. I wanted to see it with an audience. Obviously, I saw cuts of it [before]. Telluride was the first time I saw it. It is difficult to watch, yeah.

I never watched the dailies on set when I'm acting, because it's so distracting in some ways. Sometimes I would watch it to see what the frame might be, but I never look at it in relation to the performance. But actually I really, really immersed myself in it more than ever. I always do a little bit, but this one was so intense. It was a quick shoot for what we had to cover comparatively. I think it was maybe six weeks. It's a lot. And Ian was in every single scene. And there's so many beats you have to hit in some ways, and the performance, and the tracking of his illness. And some days, because of the constraints of the budget, you have to be ill in the morning and healthy in the afternoon. And your appearance was changing, which could be difficult, but it meant that we were able to get the actors that we wanted, rather than schedule it out so that it would be easy.

If we were going to get Olivia Colman or we were going to get Billie or Johnny Flynn or whoever, we'd prioritize getting them, and so we would get the actors when we needed them. And if that meant we had to change rather than just doing a chronological decline, so to speak, that's what we tried to do. So, I decided that I was going to make it fun, trying to make it fun, because one of the things about Ian was that he was enormously fun kind of guy. It's what everybody said about him.

DEADLINE: You learned that from his family and friends?

SCOTT: Yeah. Everybody who encountered him, that's what the first thing they'd say, that he was very sparkly and kind of flirtatious and just had a great sense of humor. And it was a tough road to get the film made as it is. So, actually just being on set, I was just delighted to be there. I was like, "Yes, this is happening. Here everybody is."

The last time we spoke was just after mum died and it definitely, without a doubt, fueled the passion behind this project. There's no doubt about it. It occurred to me, as we were moving on with the development of the film, that I was really, really attached to it, because there were so many things in it that I felt I could relate to about mortality and about identity, sexual and otherwise. Shakespeare, the theater, The National Theatre, actors, love, all those things. And so, I just got more and more involved in it. Even though I feel a little bit heartbroken that mum isn't here to watch it, because she'd be so proud and she'd love it. In some ways, I don't think going into studios and into financiers, I can remember that now. I was a man on a mission, because I feel like when you have a loss like that, as you know, you have nothing else to lose.

DEADLINE: You’ve got to keep moving too.

SCOTT: You go, “I'm going to do this, because time is a-marching on.” And if not now, when? If not now, when? And is there going to be a project which I feel more passionate than this? I don't think so — you can say, “little do I know,” but certainly up ‘til now. And then you watch it and you go “Ok that’s quite a lot.” But I enjoyed it in some ways. After we’d do big, long days, and because there was a certain weight, frankly, that I had to be at, I used to go to the gym in the evening. I used to walk home, because on sets you don't move. I used to walk home and then I would learn whatever soliloquy or whatever it was on the way home. And even though it was incredibly intense in the middle of the winter, there's something where you just go, "I'm going to immerse myself in this and pretty much this alone." It's a kind of privilege to be able to get to do that. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

DEADLINE: I was speaking to a friend recently about how work can very easily become our whole lives, and I was thinking about that Mary Oliver quote, “Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?” And the idea of, did anyone on their deathbed ever wish they’d worked more, rather than loved more or had more fun? But then I thought, actually Ian did, because work seems like a vocation for him. Is it like that for you?

SCOTT: Sometimes it's vocational. And I think it's really interesting to hear you say that. There are certain projects that are vocational and there are certain things, certainly over the past couple of years, where I think I've used work to keep my head afloat. One, there were certain financial obligations that I have in my family that I want to honor and all that stuff, and two, because it gives you structure. After I did Elsinore, I made another film and there was a lot of work around that time.

DEADLINE: Walk the Blue Fields with Emily Blunt?

SCOTT: Yeah [laughs. I can't say her name without laughing, because she's so much fun. She just sent me a hysterical voice note. Isn't that the power of Emily Blunt? Say her name and I start to laugh. But anyway, you have to start thinking as my birthday approached and all that stuff, you think, "OK, but what else? What are the other things that you could apply this kind of energy to your life?" And not everything can be vocational.

Doing a job like Elsinore has to affect your health in some ways. Or doing plays like Vanya . I never really stopped all that time. And after I did Vanya actually, I was unwell after that for a while. I had to affect having a panic attack in that play. For about the last two weeks of the run, I started [having panic attacks for real]. For about six weeks after, I thought, wow, your body just doesn't know the difference. So, to unlearn it, I was checking my [heart rate]. I got an Apple watch. I don't know if you ever had a panic attack, but it feels like you're going to have a heart attack, and then you check your [vitals], and you go, "No, that's not happening. That's not happening."

SCOTT: [The waiter hands him the protein smoothie he ordered.] Thank you. Back in the day we’d be having a martini.

DEADLINE: What's happened to us?

SCOTT: I know. So, anyway, yeah, what you say about vocation is really true. And I do feel that. I do feel like some things, those things, will really light you up. I'm pretty good at making the wildness of this job, and the travel, and the jet lag, and the endlessness of it, trying to see the fun of it, because it is fun.

DEADLINE: The reality is though that you are constantly on the move and dealing with jetlag…

SCOTT: And then they just paint you and they push you on the red carpet [laughs]. God knows, I’m not complaining. I'm really not. My god. You do think, this is fun. And because as an actor, you want to take your opportunities, this is bliss. And actually, when I was really exhausted coming from Elsinore , I remember arriving in Dublin. I’d been to the South by Southwest Festival in Austin, Texas and I came back and went to rehearse with Emily in Dublin. The costume designer told me weeks later, "I sort of exhaled and inhaled, because you just looked so awful.” And it was because I just hadn’t slept or whatever. But then you go and you start working with divine people like Emily Blunt and Ciarán Hines and John Crowley. I just had a ball. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid5' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

DEADLINE: I’m looking forward to seeing that.

SCOTT: Emily is a very, very special person. Have you met her?

DEADLINE: Yes. I love her humor. Watching Elsinore, I get this massive bolt of nostalgia being British, because British people, and, not to speak for you, but I think Irish people too, have such a thing for undercutting sadness with humor, it's Fleaba g humor. It's the way that Ian talks and there's always this thing of, "Don't get too sad, because I'm going to hit you with something rude." And Emily's humor…

SCOTT: …is exactly like that. Sometimes the kindest thing you can do when someone gives you bad news is not to give them a hug. The kindest, most sensitive thing to do is to make fun of them.That's why I love Stephen's script. When Ian comes out to the company [telling them he has AIDS], they say, "Well, you're the only person in the company who hasn't bought any biscuits."That's so great. What a line. And, "You’re always drawing attention to yourself.” And then everybody’s always laughing, because it's so wildly inappropriate. I love the daring of that. I love that that is what actors are like. All the best people in my life, in fact, I think the loves of my life really, have been people like that, that dare to say the unsayable and are courageous in that way.

Acting is a much-derided profession and sometimes quite rightly, but I love the idea that acting is of use to people, that for people who can't express themselves that way, someone else will do that, and will be vulnerable in front of 1,000 people in order to do something that I think is a service in the world. Of course, it's not rocket science, but it isn't meaningless and it is a great use to people.

DEADLINE: I think the only thing that truly changes people's minds is art and storytelling.

SCOTT: I totally agree. And I always think of during the pandemic, the first thing we went to was the arts. What are you listening to? What boxset are you watching? What film are you watching? What book are you reading? That's why it's got to be treated seriously. That's why it should be for everybody.

articles.title: The 25 Best New York Movies of All Time, Ranked
articles.summary: In honor of three true-blooded New York features currently in theaters, THR film critics — two of them born-and-raised NYC natives — pick their all-time favorites from a subgenre as rich and varied as the city itself.
articles.content:
Set against the background of rapidly gentrifying 1990s New York — Brooklyn and Harlem in particular — debuting director A.V. Rockwell’s atmospherically charged Sundance winner gives Teyana Taylor a powerhouse showcase as Inez, a hair stylist and single mother fresh from a stint at Rikers and determined to get her 6-year-old boy out of the foster care system by whatever means necessary.

Tracing a decade-plus in the marginalized lives of the mother and son, this moving character study watches Inez evolve from youthful bravado to hard-won self-possession. It also acutely observes painful rips in the fabric of New York City life for the economically disadvantaged and racial minorities, under the aggressive policies of Rudy Giuliani’s mayoral administration and on through the rampant development and discriminatory policing of the Bloomberg years.

Queens native James Gray made a trio of dark and eloquent outer-borough thrillers ( Little Odessa , The Yards , We Own the Night ) before switching gears with this romantic drama set in Brighton Beach — about as far as you can get from Manhattan without officially leaving New York City. The neighborhood’s windswept boardwalks and beaches are a perfect backdrop for a searing study of desire, in which a 30-something homebody (Joaquin Phoenix) is caught between two women: the nice local Jewish girl (Vinessa Shaw) that his parents want him to marry and the bewitching blond shiksa ( Gwyneth Paltrow ) that he spies on, Rear Window -style, from across the courtyard of their apartment building.

With a mastery of tone and an eye for authentic detail, Gray turns the setup for a zany rom-com into an arrestingly intimate tale of longing anchored by three great performances. Set to the swooning arias of Puccini and Mascagni, the film takes on the emotional proportions of a small-scale Brooklyn opera by the final act.

Peter Sollett’s film is not only a radiant and delicate indie rom-com/coming-of-ager, in which a 16-year-old self-styled lothario (Victor Rasuk) learns to be worthy of his guarded, regally dignified crush (Judy Marte). It’s also an indelible portrait of the Lower East Side’s Dominican community that vividly captures the romantic glow and sweaty, sensual restlessness of summer in the city. From the cacophony of a public pool on a scorching day, to the cramped apartment where the protagonist spars with his siblings and grandma, to tender close-ups of the teenage characters seducing, rebuffing, confronting and then tentatively yielding to each other, it’s a modest movie that nonetheless brims with authentic New York swagger and soul.

Revolving around a longtime gay couple (John Lithgow and Alfred Molina at their rumpled best) forced to sell their West Village apartment — and make less-than-ideal sleeping arrangements — when one of them is fired from his job, Ira Sachs’ understated heartbreaker is also an ode to the glories, aggravations and absurdities of life in the city. Lovingly shot and precisely observed, the film is imbued with a weary affection for a metropolis that’s changed in cruel ways but retains its inexorable pull on so many of the eccentric, creative people who call it home — and go to often logic-defying lengths to do so.

This is a movie that grasps the socioeconomic and logistical challenges of 21st century New York City (from daunting subsidized housing applications to the awkwardness of hosting guests in small apartments), folding them into an achingly wise story about loss, legacy and the imperfect ways we love one another, in life and beyond.

Made in an era when hijacking planes was a frequent occurrence, Joseph Sargent’s raw and riveting adaptation of a novel by John Godey (real name Morton Freedgood) revolves around an almost ridiculous premise: Bad guys hijack a subway car and threaten to kill one passenger per minute if the city doesn’t cough up $1 million in used bills within an hour.

But the bad guys weren’t counting on the perspicacity of Transit Police Lieutenant Zachary Garber (Walter Matthau at his most deliciously Matthau-ian), among others. The dialogue’s abundant racism hasn’t aged well, and the command center’s walls of blinking Christmas light bulbs look absurdly quaint. But there’s real, palpable New York City grit in the movie — literally so, in the grimy tunnels used as locations standing in for the 28th Street station, where the titular 6 train stops while negotiations proceed over walkie-talkies between Matthau’s officer and the lead hijacker (a silken Robert Shaw). Watch and marvel at how fast the cops get across lower Manhattan traffic in order to hit the deadline.

Before the Lower East Side became an overpriced haven for hipsters, fashionistas and finance bros, its streets were lined with modest mom-and-pop businesses, many of them run by Jewish New Yorkers whose families had settled there at the turn of the 19th century. The last remnants of that Manhattan shtetl are lovingly portrayed in Joan Micklin Silver’s charming rom-com, which follows a bookshop employee (Amy Irving) and a pickle vendor (Peter Riegert) who can’t manage to hook up despite the pair of matchmaking bubbes trying to get them together.

Adapted by Susan Sandler from her own play, the film captures a vibrant pre-Giuliani-era LES, in which working- and middle-class 30-somethings could still afford to pay the rent and, perhaps, fall in love. (Micklin Silver’s memorable debut, Hester Street , depicts the very same neighborhood back in 1896, when Jewish immigrants were first building a community that has all but disappeared by now.)

The fact that Noah Baumbach ’s sharp, affectionate portrait of a very modern millennial woman (Greta Gerwig, also co-writer) is filmed in knowingly retro black-and-white is just one of its many charming contradictions, along with the way its sketch-comedy randomness builds to a perfect, cohesive ending. The monochrome palette also signifies that this is a particular kind of New York movie, harking back to screwball comedies and vintage Woody Allen. The city is a playground for the not-quite-grown-up heroine, and Baumbach and Gerwig punctuate Frances’ odyssey through it with title cards noting each address she comes to rest at — from the Prospect Park digs she starts out sharing with her bestie (Mickey Sumner) to the room in a Chinatown walk-up that she rents from more moneyed hipsters (Adam Driver, Michael Zegen) and beyond.

Frances, a disorganized dancer struggling to find her footing in the performance world, literally prances and pirouettes through city streets in immaculately edited montages cut to pop classics like David Bowie’s “Modern Love.” You can’t help but fall in love with her at least a bit, as well as seeing how clearly Frances’ journey augurs Gerwig’s own eventual transition from ingenue to confident writer-director.

While Spike Lee’s The 25th Hour captured the rage and chaos of post-9/11 New York, the film that best channeled that period’s deep-seated malaise was Kenneth Lonergan’s maligned, underseen, then critically resurrected coming-of-age drama Margaret . For this epically intimate story of a teenage girl (played by a remarkable Anna Paquin) whose life is upended after she witnesses a fatal bus accident, Bronx-born Lonergan chose to stage the action on the Upper West Side, populating his film with well-educated, upper-middle-class Manhattanites facing the consequences of a gruesome death that could have perhaps been avoided.

Shot in 2005 but then mired in legal and editing-room disputes for years, the film only hit theatres in 2011, by which time many New Yorkers had tried to put Sept. 11 behind them. More than a decade later, Margaret remains a rich and unsettling portrait of a time when the city suddenly lost its mojo — a sentiment echoed by the film’s 17-year-old heroine, who can’t shake off her sense of guilt, or the feeling that the world has suddenly fallen to pieces.

This exhilarating post-World War II MGM classic musical is packed with top-name talents both in front of and behind the camera. Co-star Gene Kelly choreographed it and co-directed with Stanley Donen, the first of many fruitful collabs between the two. Meanwhile, Kelly is one of a trio of male leads, alongside Frank Sinatra and Broadway star Jules Munshin, who play three sailors maximizing their fun on a 24-hour shore leave. The lads link up via a series of very New York encounters with three women (or “goyles”): a horny cab driver (Betty Garrett), an anthropologist (super-hoofer Ann Miller) and an aspiring model-dancer (Vera-Ellen).

Kelly and Donen insisted that they film on location at least a little bit, which means the cityscape of 1949 Columbus Circle is on full display, as are other locales. The city’s eternally changing nature forms a key component of the plot, toasted in songs like “New York, New York” and “Come Up to My Place,” wherein Sinatra’s character keeps asking to visit long-gone tourist attractions. Now the then-modish spots they do visit seem just as antiquated and historical as the Hippodrome.

A good chunk of Susan Seidelman’s delightful screwball mistaken-identity comedy unfolds in bougie Fort Lee, New Jersey. But the movie’s punk heart beats loudest in downtown New York, where Roberta, a bored housewife played by Rosanna Arquette, gets a bump on the head in Battery Park and becomes convinced she’s Susan, a bohemian scenester played by Madonna in her first and best major screen role. Still in her ascendance when the film was shot, the pop star’s signature sense of style informed the character and became influential in ’80s fashion.

Locations featured include the former cult East Village vintage clothing store Love Saves the Day, the Bleecker Street Cinema and hot night spot Danceteria, while Washington Heights’ Audubon Ballroom stood in for fictional dive Magic Club (John Turturro plays the emcee). And Seidelman peppered the cast with downtown artists including Rockets Redglare, Annie Golden, John Lurie, Ann Magnuson and Shirley Stoler, and included a cameo from the adult triplets whose astonishing history was recounted in 2018 doc Three Identical Strangers . The Village Voice personal ads play a significant role, but MVP is Laurie Metcalf, in sublimely acerbic form as Roberta’s judgy sister-in-law.

This funny and achingly felt film is an artifact of the times, as one of the first to engage with AIDS and its impact (writer-director Bill Sherwood himself died of the disease four years after this, his only feature-length work, was released). But it’s also an admirably expansive work that takes a snapshot of New York life on a broader scale. At the center, there’s a love triangle of sorts, between couple Michael (Richard Ganoung) and Robert (John Bloger) and Michael’s rock-musician ex Nick (an inconceivably young Steve Buscemi), who is HIV positive. The night before Michael leaves for a six-month work assignment in Africa, he and Robert attend a dinner party thrown by a married man and woman with their own sexual secrets and then another soiree downtown hosted by their artist friend (Kathy Kinney).

Sherwood and his cast limn these different milieus with the lightest of brushstrokes, bringing in a galaxy of vividly realized characters to populate the overlapping realms. This is a scruffy New York on the back foot in the era of Mayor Ed Koch, seething with anger and creativity that’s not yet been priced out by Wall Street money.

A razor-sharp depiction of the kind of soul-crushing corporate culture and patriarchal entitlement that decades later would become the language of Mad Men , Billy Wilder’s evergreen 1960 romantic comedy is shot through with an expressive vein of melancholy. Jack Lemmon stars as Baxter, an insurance clerk who mistakenly believes career advancement will be his reward for handing over the key to his Upper West Side apartment multiple nights a week to married company executives in need of a place to carouse with their mistresses. Among them is Fred MacMurray’s head of personnel, whose affair with elevator operator Fran Kubelik — one of Shirley MacLaine’s most cherished performances — hits a bump when she attempts suicide with an overdose of sleeping pills in Baxter’s apartment.

While much of the shoot took place on a Hollywood studio lot, this is a quintessential NYC movie, from its portrayal of the midcentury workplace grind to its tender insights into urban solitude, notably in Baxter’s line from the exquisite closing scene: “I used to live like Robinson Crusoe. I mean shipwrecked among 8 million people.”

What Jean-Luc Godard’s first feature, Breathless , was to New Wave-era Paris, John Cassavetes’ jazzy and downbeat Shadows was to Beat-era New York City. Both were made in the late ’50s and both broke directing norms, helping launch movements — the Nouvelle Vague in France, independent filmmaking in the U.S. — that changed the face of cinema.

But whereas Godard’s film was a tongue-in-cheek homage to film noir and Hollywood, Cassavetes’ hip, deeply felt drama tackled tensions in a city divided along racial lines, even if it wasn’t technically segregated. The project stemmed from theater workshops the actor-director conducted with aspiring young talents in Manhattan, and that improvised approach lent it a striking realism compared to most American films of the time. Shadows still resonates powerfully through its honest portrait of three Black siblings — two of them light-skinned — trying to make it as musicians and writers in New York, which also means trying to overcome biases that were prevalent back then and haven’t yet been definitively erased.

Big Apple realtors like to claim “location is everything” while selling overpriced, closet-sized apartments to folks dying to live in one of the city’s coveted ZIP codes. Such a tagline could also be applied to William Friedkin ’s heart-pounding NYC cop thriller, which set a standard for action flicks that has rarely been equaled ever since the film triumphed at the box office and Oscars more than 50 years ago.

Friedkin broke lots of rules — as well as several laws — during the shoot, sending stunt drivers down pedestrian-lined Brooklyn streets or bribing an MTA official for a mind-boggling subway chase toward the end of the movie. The result was a sustained game of cat and mouse that literally hits the ground running and never lets up until the credits roll. By then, we’ve raced through three out of five boroughs in a pursuit that feels both visceral and existential, making us question whether the movie’s obsessive pair of NYPD detectives (a never-better Gene Hackman and Roy Scheider ) have been chasing phantoms the entire time.

Of the many qualities that contributed to the immense success of The Godfather , the authenticity of its setting is seldom mentioned. And yet unlike most mob movies before it, Francis Ford Coppola’s crime classic was shot entirely on location in New York City (except for sequences set in L.A. and Sicily), lending it a verisimilitude that made the travails of the Corleone clan feel both real and Shakespearean.

Working with twice the budget and the full blessing of Paramount, Coppola went bigger and broader for the film’s brilliant sequel, hopping across several continents and time periods for a three-plus-hour epic set simultaneously in the 1950s and the 1920s. For the latter part, which traces the rise of Vito Corleone (Robert De Niro) from Sicilian immigrant to all-powerful Don, the director — along with DP Gordon Willis and production designer Dean Tavoularis — took several streets on Manhattan’s East Village through a time warp. The result was a stunning re-creation of classic Little Italy, as well as one of cinema’s great murder scenes.

One of the all-time great movies about New York City as the nation’s vibrant theater hub, Joseph L. Mankiewicz’s delectably witty 1950 backstage drama left such a mark that calling someone “an Eve Harrington” — after the rapacious title character played by Anne Baxter — remains widely understood code for the kind of ruthlessly ambitious upstart who would step over your corpse to climb the ladder. Insinuating herself into the life of Broadway legend Margo Channing, one of Bette Davis’ defining roles, Eve poses as the meekest, most devoted of fans while plotting each maneuver that gets her closer to becoming a grand leading lady of the stage. She’s the ultimate protégée as predator.

In the bright lights of Broadway, the stage-door alleys, sophisticated cocktail parties and self-congratulatory awards ceremonies, the film captures a moment when New York theater was considered the epicenter of American culture. For those of us who chose a career as critics, it also has the magnificent George Sanders as Addison DeWitt, a viper-tongued drama critic with make-or-break influence, whose perceptiveness allows him to see through Eve and exert control over her, even as he helps clear her path to stardom.

No movie nails the boozy, sophisticated and sinister ambiance of post-war midtown Manhattan like Alexander Mackendrick’s scathing New York noir. Inspired by the antics of legendary gossip columnist Walter Winchell and publicist Irving Hoffman (who wrote regularly for The Hollywood Reporter ), this sharp-tongued look at journalism, celebrity, cutthroat competition and backstabbing New Yawkas features a murderers’ row of talent both in front of and behind the camera: stars Tony Curtis and Burt Lancaster; writers Clifford Odets and Ernest Lehman; a score by Elmer Bernstein; and cinematography by the great James Wong Howe, who captures the city — mostly Times Square and its surroundings — in vibrant chiaroscuro black-and-white.

Famous for its machine gun one-liners, delivered like disses in a rap battle a few decades before New York would invent hip-hop, the film is best summed up by what Lancaster’s J.J. Hunsecker says before he climbs into a cab after another night of making and breaking people with the stroke of his pen: “I love this dirty town.”

Is there a more iconic New York movie moment than Audrey Hepburn’s Holly Golightly, resplendent in a black Givenchy evening gown, stepping out of a yellow cab onto Fifth Avenue in the early morning hours, sipping takeout coffee and nibbling on a Danish while gazing at the window displays of the famed jewelry emporium?

Blake Edwards’ 1961 film of the Truman Capote novel shows its age in Mickey Rooney’s cartoonish ethnic stereotype as Holly’s Japanese photographer neighbor Mr. Yunioshi. But it nonetheless remains an enchanting portrait — both cynically transactional and romantic — of the city as a sanctuary for a self-invented social butterfly living off wealthy men and a handsome young aspiring writer reliant on the “patronage” of a well-heeled woman (all hail Patricia Neal). The boozy party in Holly’s East 71st Street brownstone is one for the ages, eventually shut down by cops, but not before willowy model Mag Wildwood crashes drunkenly to the floor like a felled tree.

Beyond Woody Allen, there’s perhaps no director more synonymous with the Big Apple than Martin Scorsese, who was born in Queens and grew up in Little Italy — a neighborhood that would shape him as an artist and serve as a backdrop for his earliest features. Several Scorsese flicks ( Mean Streets , Raging Bull , After Hours , Goodfellas , The Age of Innocence ) could easily have made our list, but the one that feels the most indelibly New York-y of them all is Taxi Driver . This may be because the movie nearly plays like a documentary, bringing to deeply unsettling life the grimy, horny, crime-ridden streets of Times Square, Hell’s Kitchen and other Manhattan enclaves during the dog days of the 1970s — when the Daily News famously quipped that President Gerald Ford had told the city to “drop dead.”

But Taxi Driver is as much a N.Y. of the mind as it is of the eye, channeling the inner solitude of its antihero, Travis Bickle, a perennial outsider who lives by night in a town that never sleeps, viewing it as either fantasy or hellscape from the safety of his cab.

Anyone who has lived in a Manhattan courtyard apartment block or has a clear view into homes across the street knows the unplanned voyeuristic pleasures of catching neighbors doing weird shit. In the case of Alfred Hitchcock’s riveting murder mystery — among the filmmaker’s very best — James Stewart’s Jeff is the observer, a photojournalist immobilized by a busted leg who becomes convinced that a lugubrious-looking traveling salesman in the building opposite his Greenwich Village home has killed his bedridden wife. Unable to convince his detective pal of foul play, Jeff enlists his wisecracking home nurse, Stella (peak Thelma Ritter), and glamorous model girlfriend, Lisa (Grace Kelly, dripping couture), in his amateur sleuthing.

Shot almost entirely inside and through the windows of Jeff’s apartment, the movie makes masterful use of subjective camera. It also vividly evokes the kind of sweltering heat wave — without air-conditioning — that might make any New Yorker contemplate murder.

With the Godfather trilogy, The Panic in Needle Park , Serpico , Cruising and Carlito’s Way , among others, Al Pacino almost merits his own personal NYC movie ranking. Unforgettably paired here with John Cazale — one of just five features in the brief but blazing career of the great character actor, who died at 42 — they play Sonny and Sal, inexperienced crooks attempting in 1972 to rob the First Brooklyn Savings Bank, in part to pay for the gender-affirming surgery of Sonny’s lover, Leon.

Sidney Lumet’s gritty thriller is steeped in the kind of unbearably tense, restless pressure-cooker atmosphere that's typical of a sweltering New York City summer. Based on a real-life heist-and-hostage situation, the film unfolds with both irreverent humor and searing compassion as the naïve would-be robbers watch the situation spiral out of control over the course of eight sweaty hours, becoming a media circus that builds to preordained tragedy at Kennedy airport. Standouts among the deep bench of outstanding supporting players are Charles Durning as the cops’ empathetic primary negotiator, Susan Peretz as Sonny’s emotionally volatile wife and Chris Sarandon as Leon, his eyes brimming with raw pain and exhaustion through a semi-improvised farewell phone call.

Many of us would love a spacious two-bedroom Upper West Side apartment — but maybe not the one where Mia Farrow’s title character, an expectant mother, lives with her husband, a theater actor struggling to get a foothold on Broadway (played with an incremental drip of subtle menace by John Cassavetes). Then there’s the neighbor (the inimitable Ruth Gordon), a seemingly benign eccentric who’s a tad too solicitous to be genuine.

While the exteriors of Roman Polanski’s ageless psychological chiller were filmed at the famed Dakota Apartments facing Central Park, interiors were shot on Paramount soundstages in Los Angeles. But this enthrallingly insidious tale of women’s bodily autonomy, paranoia, lapsed-Catholic hysteria and Satanism lives and breathes residential Manhattan — namely, the unsettling side of apartment-building living, in close proximity to complete strangers. The film includes a nail-biting scene in which pregnant Rosemary wanders through oncoming midtown traffic in a daze, captured by Polanski himself with a handheld camera since no crewmembers were willing to risk their lives on a busy street not closed off for shooting.

Robert Wise and Jerome Robbins’ outstanding, canonical movie musical — a grafting of Romeo and Juliet onto a pre-gentrification Upper West Side — improves on the 1957 Broadway hit right off the bat: The exhilaratingly staged “Prologue” and “Jet Song” use aerial footage of 1961 New York, coming down to land just north of the San Juan Hill (now Lincoln Square) area, where the Sharks and Jets express their enmity with finger clicks and elegant jetés through eerily empty streets.

The romantic tragedy at the film’s center is timeless, but this West Side Story also bottles up a stylized version of the period’s working-class New York culture and ethnic strife (Puerto Rican immigrants versus mainland-born whites) with warmth, emotion and wit — the latter expressed particularly well through Stephen Sondheim’s droll lyrics for numbers like “Gee, Officer Krupke” (“I’m depraved on account I’m deprived!”). Even the soundstage sets evoke the stark lines and scruffy textures of that midcentury concrete landscape.

Does the still-contested cancellation of Woody Allen mean we can’t still love Annie Hall ? Of all his movies, losing this one would hurt the most. Manhattan , as the name suggests, might be his most echt New York film, but the Allen character’s deeply icky romance with Mariel Hemingway’s high schooler is a punch-bowl turd you can’t ignore. Annie Hall , in which Allen’s Alvy Singer is in love with a woman nearly his own age — an indelible, never-more-charming Diane Keaton — is every bit as much a mash note to the city as it is to the characters’ relationship, which Alvy likens to a shark that must keep moving lest it die.

The metropolis we see here, full of real residents’ favorite spots, is never at risk of ceasing its perpetual motion, its constant churn of characters and kookiness becoming part of the film’s laugh-laced, bittersweet momentum. Where else could you pull Marshall McLuhan out of nowhere to solve an argument in a line to buy movie tickets? Sure, it’s a gag, but it’s rooted in a deeper truth — that that sort of thing could only happen in New York. The film’s cruelest jabs are reserved not for a person, but for the entire city of Los Angeles, a place whose only redeeming feature, to paraphrase Alvy, is that you can make a right turn on a red light.

There are many reasons Spike Lee’s third feature tops our list of the greatest New York movies, but the main one may simply be that it hasn’t aged one iota since it was shot in Brooklyn nearly 40 years ago. Part of this comes from the tragic reality that the film’s climactic event — the killing of Radio Raheem (Bill Nunn), who is choked to death by the NYPD — has been echoed many times over since the movie first came out, whether it was Eric Garner in Staten Island, Freddie Gray in Baltimore or George Floyd in Minneapolis.

Racial friction and police brutality are at the heart of Do the Right Thing , whose story depicts one long and languid NYC summer day during which tensions simmer, boil over and eventually ignite, tearing the diverse working-class neighborhood of Bedford-Stuyvesant apart. As a native Brooklynite, Lee knew some of these tensions firsthand, turning several actual incidents that rocked the Big Apple into a brilliant, hip-hop-infused ensemble piece (aside from Lee, the stacked cast includes Danny Aiello, Rosie Perez, John Turturro, Samuel L. Jackson, Giancarlo Esposito, Ossie Davis and Ruby Dee) that gradually takes on the force of a Greek tragedy.

But what really makes the movie still crackle decades later is how Lee counterbalances all the conflict and chaos with lots of streetwise humor and brotherly love, highlighting the resilience that New Yorkers can show in the face of a crisis. His film is a love letter to the town he grew up in, even if it’s one dipped in blood, sweat and broken glass. It’s New York as melting pot, salad bowl, powder keg and barrel of laughs. New York as America.

Though, I couldn't recommend that you visit these spots with other friends and family in the room as things could get a little awkward.

There is a grand total of three strip clubs in GTA 6 , as far as we know, two of which are located in Vice City. We've provided the locations of each of these clubs for you below. Should more clubs become available, we'll update the information below. If you intend to make the trip to any one of these locations, be prepared to spend some of your hard-earned dollars.

There are three strip clubs of note in GTA 6 . They are as follows:

If you're looking for a good time, Jack of Hearts might actually be the best highlight when it comes to Strip Clubs. You can find it in Crosstown in the heart of Vice City. It's often packed and has the quintessential nightlife energy that one might be looking for. Its vibrant atmosphere, including hip-hop music and flashy neon themes, makes it one of the liveliest destinations in Vice City.

While in a strip club, there are a few activities you can engage in. Of course, you can knock back a few drinks for those fun stat boosts. Sometimes, you can dance with your partner. This is one of those relationship-building activities that might be worthwhile. And obviously, you can pay for private dances whether you're playing as Jason or Lucia. You'll have to find an ATM as you can only pay in cash. There is likely one close by in the club. There'll be a fee for the dance, and then you can pay more for tips. Players will be able to request the same stripper when returning or select a "surprise me" option.

So, should you wish to partake in some of Vice City's more adult-oriented entertainment, you're not short on options. Even though some fans are disappointed that the prostitution staple of the series (since GTA III ) is no longer available in GTA 6 , you can still engage in some legal promiscuous activity.

articles.title: The DCU Is Going Through Big Changes, But These 5 Alternate Earths Deserve a Place in Its Future
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of DC Comics The DCU is in flux right now. Warner Brothers Discovery was bought by SkyDance and DC Studio heads James Gunn and Peter Safran were let go. SkyDance has a very different way of looking at the world than the former heads of DC Studios and many DC fans aren't looking forward to what we're about […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The DCU is in flux right now. Warner Brothers Discovery was bought by SkyDance and DC Studio heads James Gunn and Peter Safran were let go. SkyDance has a very different way of looking at the world than the former heads of DC Studios and many DC fans aren't looking forward to what we're about to get, which is going to be headed by former MCU producer Jeremy Latcham. DC Comics is the original home of the superhero and the fact that its cinematic universes have had so many problems is frustrating for a lot of fans. The DCU looked to be something different, because Gunn understood what DC is, but as usual in the real world, money always wins.

DC Comics created a multiverse full of hope, with Superman at its center, and one thing that the DCU was missing was the multiverse. DC made multiverses popular and the fact that we got none of those alternate Earths in the movies is sad. DC has always been home to the best alternate Earths and if the DCU wants to grow, they need to bring them in. These five DC Earths need to show up on the big screen, showing fans why DC is so amazing.

Zombies became huge in comics thanks to Robert Kirkman's The Walking Dead and Marvel Zombies . DC would join the zombie comic craze with 2010's Blackest Night , and then would leave the undead alone until 2019's DCeased . This book saw the Anti-Life Equation get into Cyborg's systems during a battle on Apokolips. When he returned to Earth, it uploaded itself into every piece of tech on the planet and began infecting people using their phones and computers. The heroes had to deal with an unending surge of the dead, leading to the sequels DCeased: A Good Day to Die, DCeased: Unkillables, DCeased: Hope at World's End, DCeased: Dead Planet, and DCeased: War of the Gods .

MCU fans got to see Marvel Zombies in animate action, so it would be perfect for the DCU to bring in their equivalent. It's a great setting for stories and it uses characters that even the most casual of DC fans would know. DC's alternate Earth game is strong and the DCeased Earth would be perfect to show new fans what the DC Multiverse can be. DC Studios is seemingly going in a more family-friendly direction, but DCeased would still be perfect for the films.

Earth-Two was the first DC Earth. I know it seems counterintuitive, but go with it. Next came Earth-One, starting in 1956's Showcase #4. The two would have their first crossover in The Flash #123, then the Justice League would meet the Justice Society in Justice League of America #21. Eight issues later, we'd get the third Earth, Earth-Three. On this Earth, evil always won. The Justice League of this world was the Crime Syndicate, with Ultraman, Owlman, Superwoman, Power Ring, and Johnny Quick in the places of Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, and the Flash. The team would become one of the most dangerous villainous forces in the multiverse.

Earth-Three has been around for over 60 years now and it's one of the most important Earths in DC history. It's a place where Lex Luthor is a superhero, fighting against the forces of evil. It's a world where the people we call villains are usually dead, because they tried to stand against the Crime Syndicate. There's so much to explore on Earth-Three and it could give the DCU numerous good stories.

DC Studios has decades of stories to adapt and many of the best of them are related to the multiverse. One of the most beloved of all time is Kingdom Come , by Mark Waid and Alex Ross. On this Earth, Superman ended up retiring as a new violent breed of heroes took over, followed by the rest of his generation. A massive disaster brings them out of retirement, but shadowy forces have decided that the last thing they want around is the Justice League, including a former ally with a plan that no one sees coming. It's a legendary story, and DC has returned to it several times over the decades.

Kingdom Come hasn't even had an animated adaptation, but that makes sense because of the art style. It's tailor-made for live-action adaptations and if the DCU wants to make a huge splash, this story is the way to go. If the new DC Studios want to reassure old fans, they need to remember this alternate Earth. It's one of DC's most important and the best way to show that the new regime cares about what the fans want.

DC Comics birthed the Silver Age of Comics in Showcase #4 and it's become one of the most important eras of the publisher. It was a new beginning for its heroes and while going back to read it now can reveal that it's not always amazing, it helped set the idea of what DC Comics was in the minds of readers. In the modern day, many creators have gone back to Silver Age DC, setting stories there and writing them in a more realistic style. These stories can be pretty excellent and one of the best of them is The New Frontier , from the late great Darwyn Cooke.

The book told the tale of the new age of heroes beginning, with Hal Jordan, Barry Allen, and the other greats of the Silver Age joining Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman in the battle against evil, as a mysterious new threat emerges from the shadows of World War II. It took place on Earth-21 and it's perfect for the new DCU. Latcham has talked about wanting to make movies that appeal to a broader audience. He means conservatives, basically, and putting out an Earth based on the '50s and '60s is something that the conservatives will love.

Earth-Two is the original home of DC's superheroes . This is the Earth where the stories took place from 1938 to 1956, with Superman, Batman, and Wonder Woman working alongside the Justice Society of America to battle evil. Earth-Two would return in 1961, with Jay Garrick showing up on Earth-One, followed by the Justice Society. From 1961 to 1986, when the old multiverse ended, Earth-Two was a favorite of fans, with books like All-Star Comics, Infinity Inc., and numerous back-up stories set on the Earth. DC tried to bring it back in 2011 during the New 52, but it faded away again.

The DC Multiverse is back in the comics, but Earth-Two doesn't really have a place anymore, since the Golden Age heroes all live on the prime Earth. However, bringing it into the DCU makes perfect sense. While we know that the history of superheroes of the DCU stretch far back into the past, we still don't know how it all worked. Bringing in Earth-Two would be a snap and could help set the DCU apart.

What alternate Earths do you think the DCU should introduce? Sound off in the comment section below.

articles.title: The Odyssey Extended Cut Chances Addressed by Chris Nolan, And the Answer Shouldn't Surprise Anyone
articles.summary: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey clocks in at 173 minutes in total, just seven minutes shy of three hours. Even with the epic length needed to tell Homer's story on an IMAX scale, it's till not even Nolan's longest movie as a filmmaker, but the spectacular runtime becomes even more impressive when you recall the film […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey clocks in at 173 minutes in total, just seven minutes shy of three hours. Even with the epic length needed to tell Homer's story on an IMAX scale, it's till not even Nolan's longest movie as a filmmaker, but the spectacular runtime becomes even more impressive when you recall the film made $1.8 billion at the global box office . Not bad for a time when our fractured attention spans are being pulled in many directions. So what if the movie was….even longer?

Extended cuts are nothing new in Hollywood; Sony just confirmed a version of Spider-Man: Brand New Day with 7 extra minutes of footage will arrive in December , but fans shouldn't expect the same to happen with The Odyssey . Speaking during a Q&A on the Universal Lot (via The Independent ), Nolan confirmed that “there’s a lot of deleted scenes scrumpled up in the wastebasket that no one will ever see," but noted that there is no sacred director's cut of The Odyssey hiding in a vault that he's waiting to spring on the public one day. In fact, he said he doesn't "believe" in director's cuts at all.

Nolan offered some extra context as to why he doesn't believe in the concept of director's cuts, in part because sometimes these alternate versions of movies arrive years after the fact. He added, “I want to stand by the film that goes out. As a writer-director, I try to do a lot of that weeding out. There aren’t many scenes that were shot. On a film like this, to spend a day shooting something on top of a mountain or in the rain or on a boat or whatever that isn’t gonna be in the film, I would really rather not do that. And so I wanna stand behind the cuts of the films that are put out there.”

Hearing Nolan talk about deleted scenes in that way, while also confirming that they're "scrumpled up in the wastebasket" sure seems to indicate that most of the cut material from The Odyssey never even made it to set, let alone shot before being left on the cutting room floor. For long time Nolan fans, this likely won't come as a surprise, since he's long had this mentality given the scope of the movies he makes, eager to waste no time on set for something that may not be necessary to the final cut.

It is interesting, given Nolan's reverence for filmmaker Stanley Kubrick, to hear him break down his personal philosophy. As film fans may know, the director was notorious for trimming elements of his movies even after release, with 2001: A Space Odyssey being trimmed by roughly 17 minutes after its world premiere, and The Shining undergoing similar restructuring by the director.

Good news for Nolan fans is that not only was the version in theaters his full vision, but the film is finally at home, arriving on home media this week. That said, The Odyssey is already slated for a return to IMAX theaters this holiday season, returning to the premium format on December 11, a week before Dune: Part Three takes the screens all for itself.

articles.title: 'I, Daniel Blake' Producer Says She Is "Bored Of Seeing Same Faces On Screen" As She Sets Out Blueprint To Revitalize Indie Movie Sector
articles.summary: Rebecca O'Brien, Ken Loach’s BAFTA-winning producing partner, has said she is "bored of seeing the same faces on screen" in lower budget movies. Delivering the Lord Richard Attenborough Memorial Address at the British Screen Forum Conference, O'Brien set out a blueprint to revitalize the indie movie sector and allow movies like Loach's to continue to […]
articles.content:
Rebecca O'Brien, Ken Loach 's BAFTA-winning producing partner, has said she is "bored of seeing the same faces on screen" in lower budget movies.

Delivering the Lord Richard Attenborough Memorial Address at the British Screen Forum Conference, O'Brien set out a blueprint to revitalize the indie movie sector and allow movies like Loach's to flourish. With Loach, she runs Sixteen Films, and she has made more than a dozen indie movies with the celebrated director.

"We need funders to be more open to casting from a wider pool," she said. "Casting super famous actors is great but it’s a myth that the marquee value is everything. I’m bored of seeing the same faces on screen. It homogenizes and unbalances these lower budget films." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News Biggest ITV Shows Like 'Love Island' & 'I'm A Celebrity' To Remain Free-To-Air Once Sky Deal Completes News BBC Deputy Boss Questions Impact Of "Creative Choices Taken On West Coast Of United States" On UK Audiences

O'Brien stressed she is "not anti-actor" but said too many stars now "believe they can increase their influence and power by becoming producers." "Yes, it’s great to develop your own projects but when it comes to actually getting them made, most actors don’t always know how to do the job of making a film," she added. "Why should they?"
